subject: physics

items.q: A student pushes on a horizontal table top through a flat pad of area 8.0 cm². The force exerted by the pad on the table is 40 N, directed at 30° to the vertical. What pressure does the pad exert on the table?
items.why:
At GCSE, pressure problems almost always involve weights resting on horizontal surfaces, where the whole force is perpendicular, so the condition is never needed and is forgotten. Resolve the force first. The component along the surface pushes sideways and produces no pressure; only the perpendicular component counts. For a force F at angle θ to the normal, P = F cos θ / A.

Working: Perpendicular component of the force: F⊥ = 40 N × cos 30° = 34.6 N. Area: A = 8.0 cm² = 8.0 × 10⁻⁴ m². P = F⊥/A = 34.6 N ÷ 8.0 × 10⁻⁴ m² = 4.33 × 10⁴ Pa ≈ 4.3 × 10⁴ Pa.
items.specStatementText: pressure as given by P = F/A where F is the force exerted perpendicular to the surface
items.working: Perpendicular component of the force: F⊥ = 40 N × cos 30° = 34.6 N. Area: A = 8.0 cm² = 8.0 × 10⁻⁴ m². P = F⊥/A = 34.6 N ÷ 8.0 × 10⁻⁴ m² = 4.33 × 10⁴ Pa ≈ 4.3 × 10⁴ Pa.

items.q: A sealed container holds a gas at a pressure of 1.0 × 10⁵ Pa. Which statement about this pressure is correct?
items.correct: The gas pushes perpendicular to every wall, exerting 1.0 × 10⁵ N on each square metre of wall.
items.misconception: The gas presses mainly on the base of the container, because gas pressure acts downwards.
items.why:
Pressure is first met as the pressure under a solid block or at the bottom of a liquid column, where weight is the cause, and 'air pressure' is described as the weight of the atmosphere. In a container of gas the weight of the gas is negligible. The pressure is caused by molecules colliding with the walls; the molecules move randomly in all directions, so they strike the top, sides and base equally and the pressure is the same on every wall.

Working: P = F/A, so F = PA = (1.0 × 10⁵ Pa)(1 m²) = 1.0 × 10⁵ N on each square metre, perpendicular to the wall.
items.specStatementText: pressure as given by P = F/A where F is the force exerted perpendicular to the surface
items.random_wrong: Pressure is a vector, so the pressures acting on opposite walls of the container cancel out.
items.working: P = F/A, so F = PA = (1.0 × 10⁵ Pa)(1 m²) = 1.0 × 10⁵ N on each square metre, perpendicular to the wall.

items.q: A cylinder contains 0.64 kg of oxygen gas, which consists of O₂ molecules. The molar mass of oxygen atoms is 16 g mol⁻¹, and N_A = 6.02 × 10²³ mol⁻¹. How many oxygen molecules are in the cylinder?
items.why:
Molar masses are always quoted in g mol⁻¹, while physics calculations use kg, and students do not check that the units cancel. Write the units in the division: n = m/M = 0.64 kg ÷ 0.032 kg mol⁻¹ = 20 mol. If the units do not cancel to mol, a conversion has been missed; the error is a factor of 1000.

Working: M(O₂) = 2 × 16 g mol⁻¹ = 32 g mol⁻¹ = 0.032 kg mol⁻¹. n = m/M = 0.64 kg ÷ 0.032 kg mol⁻¹ = 20 mol. N = nN_A = 20 mol × 6.02 × 10²³ mol⁻¹ = 1.2 × 10²⁵.
items.specStatementText: the amount of substance n as given by n = N/N_A where N is the number of molecules and N_A is the Avogadro constant
items.working: M(O₂) = 2 × 16 g mol⁻¹ = 32 g mol⁻¹ = 0.032 kg mol⁻¹. n = m/M = 0.64 kg ÷ 0.032 kg mol⁻¹ = 20 mol. N = nN_A = 20 mol × 6.02 × 10²³ mol⁻¹ = 1.2 × 10²⁵.

items.q: Which of the following is an assumption of the kinetic model of an ideal gas?
items.correct: Molecules exert no forces on one another except during collisions.
items.misconception: All the molecules move with the same speed, which increases with temperature.
items.why: Diagrams of the kinetic model draw every molecule with the same arrow length, and 'the molecules move faster' is taught as a single statement about the gas. Collisions continually redistribute kinetic energy, so at any instant some molecules are slow and some fast. This is why P = ⅓ρv² uses the mean of the squared speeds and why Kelvin temperature is proportional to the average kinetic energy.
items.specStatementText: that ideal gases are described in terms of the kinetic theory and constitute a modelled system used to approximate the behaviour of real gases
items.random_wrong: Molecules lose a small amount of kinetic energy in every collision with one another.

items.q: At room temperature and atmospheric pressure, measurements on helium agree closely with PV = nRT. A student concludes: 'Helium is an ideal gas.' Which evaluation of this conclusion is correct?
items.correct: Not justified: helium is a real gas that the model approximates closely under these conditions.
items.misconception: Justified: helium is monatomic and unreactive, and this makes it one of the ideal gases.
items.why: Textbooks say that helium 'behaves as an ideal gas' and teachers call a gas 'ideal' when it fits the equation, so the label is taken as a property of the substance rather than a description of the model under certain conditions. Helium can be liquefied (at about 4 K), which is impossible for an ideal gas. How closely any real gas follows the model depends on the conditions: at high pressure or near its boiling point even helium deviates.
items.specStatementText: that ideal gases are described in terms of the kinetic theory and constitute a modelled system used to approximate the behaviour of real gases
items.random_wrong: Not justified: helium atoms collide with one another, but ideal gas molecules do not collide.

items.q: For a fixed mass of gas, the ideal gas law PV/T = constant can be derived from three empirical gas laws. Which statement of those three laws is correct?
items.correct: PV is constant at constant T; V/T is constant at constant P; P/T is constant at constant V (T in K)
items.misconception: PV is constant at constant θ; V/θ is constant at constant P; P/θ is constant at constant V (θ in °C)
items.why: Temperatures are measured and quoted in °C in everyday life and in most experiments, and many other physics formulas involve only temperature differences, which are the same in °C and K. The laws V ∝ T and P ∝ T are proportionalities only for temperature measured from absolute zero. Heating from 10 °C to 20 °C does not double the pressure; it raises it by the factor 293/283 = 1.04. Convert every temperature to kelvin before substituting.
items.specStatementText: that the ideal gas law equation can be derived from the empirical gas laws for constant pressure, constant volume and constant temperature as given by PV/T = constant
items.random_wrong: PV, V/T and P/T each stay constant (T in K), whatever happens to the remaining variable

items.q: Air in a sealed syringe has a volume of 60 cm³ at a pressure of 1.00 × 10⁵ Pa and a temperature of 17 °C. The plunger is pushed in quickly until the volume is 20 cm³, and the air warms to 47 °C. Treat the air as an ideal gas. What is its new pressure?
items.why:
The three laws are learned as separate facts ('P is inversely proportional to V'), and the condition 'at constant temperature' is dropped when they are memorised. Check which of P, V and T change. When a gas is compressed quickly it warms, and its final pressure is higher than PV = constant predicts. Use P₁V₁/T₁ = P₂V₂/T₂, which reduces to each empirical law only when one variable is fixed.

Working: T₁ = 17 + 273 = 290 K; T₂ = 47 + 273 = 320 K. P₁V₁/T₁ = P₂V₂/T₂ gives P₂ = P₁ × (V₁/V₂) × (T₂/T₁) = 1.00 × 10⁵ Pa × (60 cm³/20 cm³) × (320 K/290 K) = 3.31 × 10⁵ Pa. (The volume units cancel in the ratio, so cm³ may be used.)
items.specStatementText: that the ideal gas law equation can be derived from the empirical gas laws for constant pressure, constant volume and constant temperature as given by PV/T = constant
items.working: T₁ = 17 + 273 = 290 K; T₂ = 47 + 273 = 320 K. P₁V₁/T₁ = P₂V₂/T₂ gives P₂ = P₁ × (V₁/V₂) × (T₂/T₁) = 1.00 × 10⁵ Pa × (60 cm³/20 cm³) × (320 K/290 K) = 3.31 × 10⁵ Pa. (The volume units cancel in the ratio, so cm³ may be used.)

items.q: On a pressure–volume diagram (pressure on the vertical axis, volume on the horizontal axis), a fixed mass of ideal gas moves from state X to state Y along a horizontal straight line. At X the volume is 3.0 × 10⁻³ m³ and the temperature is 27 °C; at Y the volume is 6.0 × 10⁻³ m³. What is the temperature at Y, and under what condition does the change X → Y take place?
items.correct: 327 °C, at constant pressure
items.misconception: 27 °C, at constant temperature
items.why:
On many graphs a horizontal line means 'no change', and 'isothermal' and 'isobaric' are similar-sounding words that students confuse on P–V diagrams. Read the axes: along a horizontal line P is fixed while V changes. Since PV/T = constant, T changes in proportion to V along such a line. Constant-temperature changes lie on curves (PV = constant) that fall more steeply at small volumes.

Working: Horizontal line on a P–V diagram: P constant. V/T = constant with T in K: T_X = 27 + 273 = 300 K; T_Y = T_X × (V_Y/V_X) = 300 K × (6.0 × 10⁻³/3.0 × 10⁻³) = 600 K = 327 °C.
items.specStatementText: that the ideal gas law equation can be derived from the empirical gas laws for constant pressure, constant volume and constant temperature as given by PV/T = constant
items.working: Horizontal line on a P–V diagram: P constant. V/T = constant with T in K: T_X = 27 + 273 = 300 K; T_Y = T_X × (V_Y/V_X) = 300 K × (6.0 × 10⁻³/3.0 × 10⁻³) = 600 K = 327 °C.

items.q: A rigid storage tank of internal volume 200 dm³ contains an ideal gas at a pressure of 3.00 × 10⁵ Pa and a temperature of 27 °C. R = 8.31 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹. What amount of gas is in the tank?
items.correct: 2.4 × 10¹ mol
items.misconception: 2.4 × 10⁴ mol
items.why:
In ratio forms such as P₁V₁/T₁ = P₂V₂/T₂ the volume units cancel, so any unit works, and students carry this habit over to PV = nRT, where R fixes the units. R contains joules, and J = Pa m³, so PV must be in Pa m³. Convert dm³ to m³ (× 10⁻³) and cm³ to m³ (× 10⁻⁶) before substituting; otherwise n is 1000 or 10⁶ times too large.

Working: V = 200 dm³ = 200 × 10⁻³ m³ = 0.200 m³; T = 27 + 273 = 300 K. n = PV/(RT) = (3.00 × 10⁵ Pa × 0.200 m³) ÷ (8.31 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹ × 300 K) = 6.00 × 10⁴ J ÷ 2493 J mol⁻¹ = 24.1 mol ≈ 2.4 × 10¹ mol.
items.specStatementText: the equations governing the behaviour of ideal gases as given by PV = Nk_B T and PV = nRT

items.q: A flask of volume 250 cm³ contains an ideal gas at a pressure of 1.0 × 10⁵ Pa and a temperature of 300 K. k_B = 1.38 × 10⁻²³ J K⁻¹, R = 8.31 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹ and N_A = 6.02 × 10²³ mol⁻¹. How many molecules are in the flask?
items.why:
Both constants appear in near-identical equations and both are called 'gas constants', so students choose whichever they remember. Match the constant to the counting unit: moles go with R, molecules go with k_B. PV/(RT) gives a number of moles, which must be multiplied by N_A to give molecules; PV/(k_B T) gives molecules directly. Since k_B = R/N_A, the two routes agree.

Working: V = 250 cm³ = 2.5 × 10⁻⁴ m³. N = PV/(k_B T) = (1.0 × 10⁵ Pa × 2.5 × 10⁻⁴ m³) ÷ (1.38 × 10⁻²³ J K⁻¹ × 300 K) = 25 J ÷ 4.14 × 10⁻²¹ J = 6.0 × 10²¹. (Check: n = PV/(RT) = 1.0 × 10⁻² mol, and nN_A = 6.0 × 10²¹.)
items.specStatementText: the equations governing the behaviour of ideal gases as given by PV = Nk_B T and PV = nRT

items.q: Two identical rigid containers are at the same temperature and the same pressure. One holds hydrogen (H₂) and the other holds carbon dioxide (CO₂). Both gases behave as ideal gases. How do the numbers of molecules in the two containers compare?
items.correct: They are equal, as equal pressure, volume and temperature mean equal numbers.
items.misconception: There are more H₂ molecules, as smaller molecules leave room for more of them.
items.why: Particle diagrams in textbooks draw gas particles large and crowded to fit the page, and students find it hard to accept that most of a gas is empty space. At room temperature and pressure the average spacing of air molecules is about ten times their diameter, so the molecules occupy roughly a thousandth of the volume. This is why gases are easily compressed and why the number of molecules in a given volume at fixed P and T does not depend on molecular size.
items.specStatementText: the equations governing the behaviour of ideal gases as given by PV = Nk_B T and PV = nRT
items.random_wrong: There are more CO₂ molecules, as the heavier gas is the larger amount of substance.

items.q: Which statement correctly explains how a gas exerts a pressure on the walls of its container?
items.correct: Each molecule's momentum changes as it rebounds from a wall, so it exerts a force on the wall.
items.misconception: The molecules repel one another, and this repulsion pushes outwards on the walls.
items.why: A gas that pushes back when compressed feels springy, and early models (including Newton's) explained gas pressure by static repulsion between particles; 'the particles push on the walls' is common everyday phrasing. In an ideal gas the molecules exert no forces on each other except during collisions, yet the gas exerts a pressure. The pressure comes from the momentum change of each molecule as it rebounds from a wall: the wall pushes the molecule back and the molecule pushes the wall out.
items.specStatementText: that the change in momentum of particles due to collisions with a given surface gives rise to pressure in gases and, from that analysis, pressure is related to the average (translational speed)² of molecules as given by P = ⅓ρv²
items.random_wrong: The weight of the molecules presses down on the container, mostly on its base.

items.q: A sample of helium at 300 K has a density of 0.160 kg m⁻³. The mean speed of its atoms is 1.26 × 10³ m s⁻¹, and the mean of the squares of their speeds is 1.87 × 10⁶ m² s⁻². Treat helium as an ideal gas. What is its pressure?
items.why:
The notation v² looks like 'v, squared', and students assume v stands for the average speed as it does in kinematics. Squaring first gives more weight to fast molecules, so the mean of the squares always exceeds the square of the mean unless every speed is the same. For example, speeds of 1 and 3 units give a mean square of 5 but a squared mean of 4. The Nov 2023 guide defines v² as the average of (translational speed)².

Working: P = ⅓ρv², with v² the mean of the squared speeds: P = ⅓ × 0.160 kg m⁻³ × 1.87 × 10⁶ m² s⁻² = 9.97 × 10⁴ Pa. The mean speed, 1.26 × 10³ m s⁻¹, is not needed.
items.specStatementText: that the change in momentum of particles due to collisions with a given surface gives rise to pressure in gases and, from that analysis, pressure is related to the average (translational speed)² of molecules as given by P = ⅓ρv²
items.working: P = ⅓ρv², with v² the mean of the squared speeds: P = ⅓ × 0.160 kg m⁻³ × 1.87 × 10⁶ m² s⁻² = 9.97 × 10⁴ Pa. The mean speed, 1.26 × 10³ m s⁻¹, is not needed.

items.q: A sealed, rigid container of ideal gas is heated. What happens to the pressure of the gas, and why?
items.correct: It rises: faster molecules hit the walls more often, each with a greater change in momentum.
items.misconception: It rises: the molecules expand when they are heated, so they strike the walls more often.
items.why: Students see materials expand when heated and attribute the macroscopic property to the individual particles, a well-documented pattern in research on particle ideas. Expansion of a material is caused by the particles moving faster and further apart, not by particles growing. In a sealed rigid container of gas, heating makes the molecules move faster, so they strike the walls more often and with a greater change of momentum each time.
items.specStatementText: that the change in momentum of particles due to collisions with a given surface gives rise to pressure in gases and, from that analysis, pressure is related to the average (translational speed)² of molecules as given by P = ⅓ρv²
items.random_wrong: It stays the same: the number of molecules per unit volume has not changed at all.

items.q: A container holds 8.0 g of helium, a monatomic gas of molar mass 4.0 g mol⁻¹, at 27 °C. Treat helium as an ideal gas. R = 8.31 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹. What is the internal energy of the helium?
items.why:
Students notice that PV and nRT come out in joules and conclude they must be 'the energy', without recalling the separate equation for U. The average translational kinetic energy per molecule is (3/2)k_B T, so for an ideal monatomic gas of N molecules U = (3/2)Nk_B T = (3/2)nRT. Leaving out the 3/2 gives an internal energy one third too small.

Working: n = m/M = 8.0 g ÷ 4.0 g mol⁻¹ = 2.0 mol; T = 27 + 273 = 300 K. U = (3/2)RnT = 1.5 × 8.31 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹ × 2.0 mol × 300 K = 7479 J ≈ 7.5 × 10³ J.
items.specStatementText: the relationship between the internal energy U of an ideal monatomic gas and the number of molecules or amount of substance as given by U = (3/2)Nk_B T or U = (3/2)RnT

items.q: A fixed mass of ideal monatomic gas is compressed slowly to half its volume while its temperature is kept constant. What happens to the internal energy U of the gas?
items.correct: It does not change, as the temperature and so the mean kinetic energy are fixed.
items.misconception: It increases, as the closer molecules store more intermolecular potential energy.
items.why:
Students picture compressing a gas like compressing a spring, and they know that internal energy in general includes intermolecular potential energy. For real substances internal energy includes intermolecular potential energy. In the ideal gas model there are no intermolecular forces, so this term is zero, and for an ideal monatomic gas U = (3/2)Nk_B T depends only on N and T.

Working: For an ideal monatomic gas U = (3/2)Nk_B T. N is fixed (fixed mass) and T is constant, so ΔU = (3/2)Nk_B ΔT = 0.
items.specStatementText: the relationship between the internal energy U of an ideal monatomic gas and the number of molecules or amount of substance as given by U = (3/2)Nk_B T or U = (3/2)RnT
items.random_wrong: It increases, because work is done on the gas while it is being compressed.
items.working: For an ideal monatomic gas U = (3/2)Nk_B T. N is fixed (fixed mass) and T is constant, so ΔU = (3/2)Nk_B ΔT = 0.

items.q: Under which conditions does a real gas behave most nearly as an ideal gas?
items.correct: High temperature, low pressure and low density
items.misconception: Low temperature, low pressure and low density
items.why: Students link 'less motion' with 'fewer interactions', and do not realise that slower molecules spend longer near each other, where attractions matter. At low temperature the molecules' kinetic energy is small compared with the intermolecular potential energy, so attractive forces noticeably affect their motion, and eventually the gas liquefies. At high temperature the attractions have a negligible effect.
items.specStatementText: the temperature, pressure and density conditions under which an ideal gas is a good approximation of a real gas.
items.random_wrong: High temperature, high pressure and high density

items.q: A real gas at a temperature a little above its boiling point is compressed to a high density. Its measured pressure is found to be lower than the value that PV = nRT predicts for the same n, V and T. Which is the best explanation?
items.correct: Attractive forces between the molecules pull those near a wall back, so they strike it with less momentum.
items.misconception: The molecules take up part of the volume, which leaves less space for the gas and so lowers its pressure.
items.why: Students know the molecular volume is one difference between real and ideal gases but reason about it as 'less gas' rather than 'less free space', which reverses the direction of the effect. Less free volume means the same molecules move in a smaller space, like a compressed gas, so the pressure is increased. When a real gas's pressure is below the ideal value, attractions between molecules are responsible: they pull molecules near a wall back into the gas and reduce the momentum they deliver.
items.specStatementText: the temperature, pressure and density conditions under which an ideal gas is a good approximation of a real gas.
items.random_wrong: Collisions between real molecules are inelastic, so the molecules slow down and the pressure falls.

items.q: Two sealed flasks each contain 0.50 mol of gas. Flask X holds helium, a monatomic gas of molar mass 4.0 g mol⁻¹. Flask Y holds nitrogen, which consists of N₂ molecules; the molar mass of nitrogen atoms is 14 g mol⁻¹. Which statement correctly compares the two samples?
items.correct: The number of N₂ molecules equals the number of He atoms, and the nitrogen has seven times the mass.
items.misconception: The number of N atoms equals the number of He atoms, and the nitrogen has 3.5 times the mass.
items.why:
Periodic tables list atomic molar masses, and students do not distinguish between an element's atoms and the molecules that make up its gas. Identify the particle being counted. The molecules of oxygen, nitrogen and hydrogen gases are diatomic (O₂, N₂, H₂), so their molar masses are double the atomic values; using the atomic value doubles the calculated number of molecules.

Working: The amount of substance counts particles: N = nN_A, so 0.50 mol of He atoms and 0.50 mol of N₂ molecules contain the same number of particles, 0.50 × 6.02 × 10²³ = 3.0 × 10²³ each.
Mass of helium = nM = 0.50 mol × 4.0 g mol⁻¹ = 2.0 g.
Molar mass of N₂ = 2 × 14 = 28 g mol⁻¹, so mass of nitrogen = 0.50 mol × 28 g mol⁻¹ = 14 g.
Ratio of masses = 14/2.0 = 7.0, so the nitrogen has seven times the mass of the helium.
items.specStatementText: the amount of substance n as given by n = N/N_A where N is the number of molecules and N_A is the Avogadro constant
items.random_wrong: The two samples have equal masses, because each flask holds the same amount of substance.
items.working:
The amount of substance counts particles: N = nN_A, so 0.50 mol of He atoms and 0.50 mol of N₂ molecules contain the same number of particles, 0.50 × 6.02 × 10²³ = 3.0 × 10²³ each.
Mass of helium = nM = 0.50 mol × 4.0 g mol⁻¹ = 2.0 g.
Molar mass of N₂ = 2 × 14 = 28 g mol⁻¹, so mass of nitrogen = 0.50 mol × 28 g mol⁻¹ = 14 g.
Ratio of masses = 14/2.0 = 7.0, so the nitrogen has seven times the mass of the helium.

items.q: When a force is at an angle θ to the vertical and pushes on a horizontal surface, is its perpendicular component F sin θ?
items.correct: No. The component perpendicular to the surface is along the vertical, which is adjacent to θ, so it is F cos θ.
items.misconception: The component 'into' a surface is always found with sin θ, whatever the angle is measured from.
items.why: Students learn a fixed pairing such as 'vertical component = F sin θ' from projectile problems, where θ is measured from the horizontal, and apply it when θ is measured from the vertical. Identify which component is adjacent to the given angle: the component adjacent to θ is F cos θ, the one opposite is F sin θ. Sketch the triangle before choosing.
items.specStatementText: pressure as given by P = F/A where F is the force exerted perpendicular to the surface
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: To convert an area or a volume to SI units, is it enough to use the conversion factor for lengths?
items.correct: No. The linear factor must be squared or cubed: 1 cm² = 10⁻⁴ m², 1 cm³ = 10⁻⁶ m³ and 1 dm³ = 10⁻³ m³.
items.misconception: Areas and volumes convert with the same factor as lengths, so cm² or cm³ become m² or m³ by dividing by 100, and dm³ become m³ by dividing by 10.
items.why: The factors for lengths (100 cm or 10 dm in a metre) are well known, and students convert the number without noticing that the unit is a square or a cube of a length. Write the unit out: 1 cm² = (10⁻² m)² = 10⁻⁴ m²; 1 cm³ = (10⁻² m)³ = 10⁻⁶ m³; 1 dm³ = (10⁻¹ m)³ = 10⁻³ m³. Using the linear factor instead leaves the answer wrong by a factor of 100 or more.
items.specStatementText: pressure as given by P = F/A where F is the force exerted perpendicular to the surface
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Is pressure a vector with a direction?
items.correct: No. Pressure is a scalar. The force that a pressure produces on a surface is a vector, directed perpendicular to that surface, but pressure itself has no direction.
items.misconception: Pressure is a vector, so pressures acting on opposite walls cancel out.
items.why: Pressure is defined from force, which is a vector, and 'pressure pushes' suggests a direction. P = F/A divides the magnitude of the perpendicular force by an area; the result has no direction. The forces on opposite walls of a container are opposite, which is why the container does not accelerate, but the pressure on each wall is the same positive value.
items.specStatementText: pressure as given by P = F/A where F is the force exerted perpendicular to the surface
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Are pressure and force the same quantity?
items.correct: No. Force is measured in N; pressure is force per unit area, in Pa = N m⁻². The force produced by a given pressure is proportional to the area: F = PA.
items.misconception: Pressure is just another word for force, so a gas at 1.0 × 10⁵ Pa exerts 1.0 × 10⁵ N on every surface, whatever its size.
items.why: In everyday speech 'pressure' and 'force' are used interchangeably ('put pressure on it'), and both are described as a push. Use F = PA. A gas at 1.0 × 10⁵ Pa exerts 1.0 × 10⁵ N on each square metre; a wall of 0.20 m² experiences 2.0 × 10⁴ N and a wall of 2.0 m² experiences 2.0 × 10⁵ N.
items.specStatementText: pressure as given by P = F/A where F is the force exerted perpendicular to the surface
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Is the amount of substance of a sample the same thing as its mass?
items.correct: No. The amount of substance n counts particles (n = N/N_A) and is measured in mol. Equal amounts of different gases contain equal numbers of molecules but have different masses.
items.misconception: The amount of substance is the mass of the sample, so a heavier sample always contains more moles and more molecules.
items.why: In everyday language 'amount' means how much stuff there is, usually measured by mass, and chemistry students first meet the mole through mass calculations. The mole is a count, like a dozen, not a mass. One mole of hydrogen molecules (2 g) and one mole of carbon dioxide molecules (44 g) contain the same number of molecules, N_A. Mass and amount are linked only through the molar mass: n = m/M.
items.specStatementText: the amount of substance n as given by n = N/N_A where N is the number of molecules and N_A is the Avogadro constant
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: In the kinetic model, do molecules lose kinetic energy when they collide with one another or with the walls?
items.correct: No. The model assumes all collisions are elastic: the total kinetic energy of the molecules is unchanged by collisions.
items.misconception: Every collision loses a little kinetic energy, so the molecules gradually slow down and the gas cools or its pressure falls.
items.why: Everyday collisions of balls and cars are inelastic and 'lose energy', and students transfer this to molecules. If molecular collisions lost energy, a sealed gas in an insulated container would cool and its pressure would fall with no energy leaving; this is not observed. Collisions change individual speeds but not the total kinetic energy.
items.specStatementText: that ideal gases are described in terms of the kinetic theory and constitute a modelled system used to approximate the behaviour of real gases
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Does 'no intermolecular forces' mean that ideal gas molecules never collide with one another?
items.correct: No. Ideal gas molecules collide with one another and with the walls; the assumption is that they exert no forces on each other EXCEPT during these brief, elastic collisions.
items.misconception: Because an ideal gas has no intermolecular forces, its molecules never interact or collide with one another; any gas whose molecules collide is not ideal.
items.why: The assumption is often shortened to 'no intermolecular forces', and simple derivations of P = ⅓ρv² ignore molecule–molecule collisions, so students conclude the model forbids them. The forces during a collision are what make it a collision. The model allows elastic collisions of negligible duration; what it excludes are forces between molecules while they are apart.
items.specStatementText: that ideal gases are described in terms of the kinetic theory and constitute a modelled system used to approximate the behaviour of real gases
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: If measurements agree with a model's predictions, does that show that the model's assumptions are exactly true?
items.correct: No. Agreement shows that the model is a good approximation under the conditions tested. A simplified model can make accurate predictions even though its assumptions are not exactly true.
items.misconception: A model that correctly predicts measurements must be an exact description of the real system, so all its assumptions hold exactly.
items.why: School science often presents models as pictures of what things are 'really like', and students are rarely shown a model that works well while being known to be simplified. The ideal gas model assumes point particles and no intermolecular forces, which is never exactly true. It predicts real-gas behaviour well when those simplifications have negligible effect (low density, high temperature) and badly when they do not. Agreement under some conditions supports the model's usefulness there, not the literal truth of its assumptions.
items.specStatementText: that ideal gases are described in terms of the kinetic theory and constitute a modelled system used to approximate the behaviour of real gases

items.q: To find a new pressure, can the old pressure simply be multiplied by 'new over old' for every other variable?
items.correct: No. A ratio must be inverted for an inversely related variable: P₂ = P₁ × (V₁/V₂) × (T₂/T₁). Pressure goes up when volume goes down.
items.misconception: Each quantity in a gas-law calculation is scaled by the ratio 'new value over old value' of every other variable.
items.why: A 'multiply by the ratio' shortcut works for direct proportionality (P ∝ T) and is applied mechanically to volume without asking whether P increases or decreases as V changes. Rearrange P₁V₁/T₁ = P₂V₂/T₂ algebraically, or reason physically: compression increases pressure, so the volume ratio must be greater than 1 when V decreases. Check the direction of each change before combining ratios.
items.specStatementText: that the ideal gas law equation can be derived from the empirical gas laws for constant pressure, constant volume and constant temperature as given by PV/T = constant
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Is every gas law an inverse proportion, like Boyle's law?
items.correct: No. Only pressure and volume are inversely related (at constant T). At constant pressure V ∝ T, and at constant volume P ∝ T: these are direct proportions.
items.misconception: All the gas laws have the same form as Boyle's law, so V × T or P × T is constant just as P × V is.
items.why: Boyle's law is usually taught first and most thoroughly, and students memorise the form 'product = constant' rather than the physical direction of each relationship. Think about the physics: heating a gas at constant pressure makes it expand, so V increases with T (V/T = constant); heating a sealed rigid container raises the pressure, so P/T = constant. Only compression at constant temperature has one quantity rising as the other falls.
items.specStatementText: that the ideal gas law equation can be derived from the empirical gas laws for constant pressure, constant volume and constant temperature as given by PV/T = constant
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Is the N in PV = Nk_B T an amount of substance in moles?
items.correct: No. N is the number of molecules, a pure count. The amount of substance in moles is n = N/N_A, which appears in PV = nRT.
items.misconception: The N in PV = Nk_B T is the amount of substance in moles, so the result must still be multiplied by N_A to give the number of molecules.
items.why: The symbols N and n look alike, and chemistry calculations usually end with 'multiply by N_A', so students add this step by habit. Check the size of the answer: a litre of gas at room conditions contains about 10²² molecules, or about 0.04 mol. PV/(k_B T) already gives the number of molecules; multiplying by N_A again gives an absurd number of order 10⁴⁶.
items.specStatementText: the equations governing the behaviour of ideal gases as given by PV = Nk_B T and PV = nRT
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: At the same temperature, does a molecule of a heavier gas exert more pressure on the walls than a molecule of a lighter gas?
items.correct: No. At the same temperature every ideal gas has the same average translational kinetic energy per molecule, (3/2)k_B T, so each molecule contributes the same pressure on average (P = Nk_B T/V does not depend on the molecular mass).
items.misconception: Heavier molecules hit the walls harder, so at the same temperature a gas of heavier molecules exerts more pressure per molecule and fewer molecules are needed for the same pressure.
items.why: Students correctly reason that a heavier molecule at the same speed transfers more momentum per collision, but forget that at the same temperature heavier molecules move more slowly. A heavier molecule has the same average kinetic energy but a lower speed: it transfers more momentum per collision but collides less often. The two effects cancel exactly, which is why PV = Nk_B T contains no molecular mass and equal volumes at the same P and T hold equal numbers of molecules.
items.specStatementText: the equations governing the behaviour of ideal gases as given by PV = Nk_B T and PV = nRT

items.q: Is the pressure of a gas the kinetic energy that its molecules give to the walls?
items.correct: No. In elastic collisions with a stationary wall the molecules keep their kinetic energy. Pressure is a force per unit area, produced by the rate of change of momentum of the molecules.
items.misconception: Molecules give up their kinetic energy to the wall when they hit it, and this energy delivered per second is the pressure.
items.why: Students link 'faster molecules' with both 'more energy' and 'more pressure' and do not distinguish momentum from kinetic energy, or force from energy. In an elastic rebound from a stationary wall the molecule's speed is unchanged, so no kinetic energy is transferred, but its momentum reverses and changes by 2mv. Force is the rate of change of momentum, and pressure is force per unit area. (Pressure has units N m⁻², which are also J m⁻³, but this does not mean it is energy delivered to the wall.)
items.specStatementText: that the change in momentum of particles due to collisions with a given surface gives rise to pressure in gases and, from that analysis, pressure is related to the average (translational speed)² of molecules as given by P = ⅓ρv²
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Why is there a factor of ⅓ in P = ⅓ρv²?
items.correct: Because the molecules move randomly in three dimensions. On average the square of the velocity component perpendicular to a given wall is one third of v².
items.misconception: All the molecules move straight towards and away from each wall, so the full v² contributes to the pressure and the ⅓ can be left out.
items.why: The derivation begins with a single molecule moving perpendicular to one wall, and students take this simplifying picture as the whole model. For random motion v² = v_x² + v_y² + v_z² on average, and the three averages are equal, so the mean of v_x² is v²/3. Only the component perpendicular to a wall contributes to the momentum change at that wall. Omitting the ⅓ makes the pressure three times too large.
items.specStatementText: that the change in momentum of particles due to collisions with a given surface gives rise to pressure in gases and, from that analysis, pressure is related to the average (translational speed)² of molecules as given by P = ⅓ρv²
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Is the coefficient in P = ⅓ρv² the same as the ½ in E_k = ½mv²?
items.correct: No. The two equations have different origins: ½ comes from kinetic energy, ⅓ from averaging random motion over three dimensions. P = ⅓ρv².
items.misconception: The pressure equation has the same form as the kinetic energy equation, so P = ½ρv².
items.why: Both equations contain a fraction multiplied by a 'mass-type' quantity and v², and E_k = ½mv² is far more familiar, so it overwrites the less familiar coefficient. Remember where the ⅓ comes from (three dimensions). Using ½ gives a pressure 1.5 times too large. Note that combining the two correctly gives PV = ⅔ × (total translational kinetic energy).
items.specStatementText: that the change in momentum of particles due to collisions with a given surface gives rise to pressure in gases and, from that analysis, pressure is related to the average (translational speed)² of molecules as given by P = ⅓ρv²

items.q: Does the pressure of a gas depend only on how many molecules there are per unit volume?
items.correct: No. Pressure also depends on how fast the molecules move: P = ⅓ρv², and v² is proportional to the absolute temperature.
items.misconception: Pressure depends only on how crowded the molecules are (the number per unit volume), so heating a sealed container does not change the pressure.
items.why: Many explanations of pressure focus on 'more particles, more collisions', especially for compression and for pumping up a tyre, so speed is left out of the picture. At constant volume the number density is fixed, but heating raises the mean square speed. Each collision then gives a larger momentum change and collisions happen more often, so the pressure rises in proportion to the kelvin temperature.
items.specStatementText: that the change in momentum of particles due to collisions with a given surface gives rise to pressure in gases and, from that analysis, pressure is related to the average (translational speed)² of molecules as given by P = ⅓ρv²
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Does doing work on a gas always increase its internal energy?
items.correct: No. The change in internal energy also depends on the energy transferred thermally. In a slow compression at constant temperature, energy equal to the work done on the gas is transferred out of it thermally, and U is unchanged.
items.misconception: Whenever work is done on a gas, for example by compressing it, its internal energy must increase.
items.why: Students learn that work transfers energy to a system and forget that energy can leave the system thermally at the same time. For an ideal gas, U depends only on T. If T is constant, U is constant, however much work is done; the work done on the gas is balanced by thermal energy transferred to the surroundings.
items.specStatementText: the relationship between the internal energy U of an ideal monatomic gas and the number of molecules or amount of substance as given by U = (3/2)Nk_B T or U = (3/2)RnT
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Does the internal energy of a gas increase when its pressure increases?
items.correct: No. For an ideal monatomic gas U = (3/2)Nk_B T depends only on the number of molecules and the absolute temperature, not on the pressure.
items.misconception: The internal energy of a gas rises when its pressure rises, because the molecules strike the walls more often.
items.why: Pressure and internal energy both rise when a sealed gas is heated, so students link them directly and also connect 'more collisions' with 'more energy'. When a gas is compressed at constant temperature its pressure rises because collisions with the walls become more frequent, but the molecules' speeds are unchanged, so their kinetic energy, and U, stay the same.
items.specStatementText: the relationship between the internal energy U of an ideal monatomic gas and the number of molecules or amount of substance as given by U = (3/2)Nk_B T or U = (3/2)RnT

items.q: Does compressing a gas to high pressure and density make it follow the kinetic model more closely?
items.correct: No. At high pressure and density the molecules are close together, so their own volume and their mutual attractions are no longer negligible, and the gas deviates more from ideal behaviour.
items.misconception: The kinetic model is about molecular collisions, so conditions with more collisions (high pressure, high density, high temperature) make a gas fit the model better.
items.why: The kinetic model is presented as a model of colliding molecules, so students assume that more collisions means more of what the model describes. The model assumes point particles with no forces between collisions. These assumptions fail when molecules are crowded together, whatever the collision rate. Low density, where molecules are far apart, is the condition for ideal behaviour.
items.specStatementText: the temperature, pressure and density conditions under which an ideal gas is a good approximation of a real gas.
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Do gas molecules stop moving when the gas is cooled close to its boiling point?
items.correct: No. Molecules move at all temperatures above absolute zero; near the boiling point they still move at hundreds of metres per second.
items.misconception: Near its boiling point a gas is so cold that its molecules almost stop moving, and they settle instead of hitting the walls.
items.why: Students associate cold with stillness, and liquids and solids are often described as having particles that 'do not move', so cooling a gas is imagined as slowing its molecules to a halt. Average kinetic energy is proportional to kelvin temperature, and at, say, 100 K it is still a third of its value at 300 K. The deviations near the boiling point arise because attractions become significant relative to this kinetic energy, not because the molecules stop.
items.specStatementText: the temperature, pressure and density conditions under which an ideal gas is a good approximation of a real gas.

items.q: Does one mole always contain the same number of particles, whatever the substance?
items.correct: Yes. One mole of any substance contains N_A = 6.02 × 10²³ particles. The amount of substance is a count of particles in units of N_A, so equal amounts of different substances contain equal numbers of particles, however different their masses.
items.misconception: One mole is a different number of particles for different substances, so a mole of a substance with heavier particles contains more (or fewer) of them.
items.why: The mole is met first through mass calculations, and 'a mole of nitrogen weighs more than a mole of helium' is easily heard as 'a mole of nitrogen is more stuff'. Studies of students' understanding of the mole concept report that many do not see the mole as a fixed number, but as a quantity that changes with the substance. Define the mole by the count: n = N/N_A. A mole of helium and a mole of nitrogen contain exactly the same number of particles, 6.02 × 10²³; the nitrogen sample is heavier only because each N₂ molecule has seven times the mass of a helium atom.
items.specStatementText: the amount of substance n as given by n = N/N_A where N is the number of molecules and N_A is the Avogadro constant
